lesson.title: Why a Crowd Can Make Help Less Likely
lesson.summary: The finding that individuals are often less likely to help someone in need when other bystanders are present than when they are the only person there, largely because responsibility for helping becomes diffused across the group.
lesson.body:
It seems intuitive that a person in trouble would be safer surrounded by more potential helpers. Research on the bystander effect shows the opposite can be true: as the number of bystanders who witness an emergency increases, each individual bystander becomes less likely, and typically slower, to help. The effect draws directly on diffusion of responsibility, since responsibility to intervene gets spread across everyone present, and on social facilitation, since being watched by others changes how confidently people act, in this case often making them more hesitant to act wrong in public rather than more capable.

The event most often connected to this research is the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese in Queens, New York. The original New York Times account, published shortly after her death, reported that 38 witnesses saw or heard the attack and did nothing to help or call police, and that story became one of the most widely repeated cases in introductory psychology for decades. It is important to know that this account has since been substantially challenged by later journalists and researchers, who found that the real number of people who directly witnessed the attack was almost certainly much smaller, that the attack itself was not a single clearly visible event but happened in stages in the dark, that at least one witness did shout at the attacker and scare him off temporarily, and that police were in fact called. The Genovese case is best understood today not as a clean factual example of bystander apathy, but as a flawed, oversimplified news story that nonetheless played a real historical role in motivating serious psychological research into why people sometimes fail to help.

That research came from John Darley and Bibb Latane, who were reportedly struck by the Genovese coverage and set out to test the underlying question experimentally rather than take the news account at face value. In one well known study, participants believed they were having a discussion over an intercom with one or several other participants, and one voice appeared to have a seizure and call for help. Participants who believed they were the only other person on the line helped quickly and at high rates, while participants who believed several other people were also on the line were slower to help and less likely to help at all, a controlled demonstration of diffusion of responsibility acting on real helping behavior rather than a self report.

Darley and Latane also proposed a decision process to explain when bystanders do and do not help, which is still taught as a useful model. A bystander must notice that something is happening, interpret it correctly as an emergency rather than something ordinary, a step complicated by pluralistic ignorance, where each bystander looks calm because they are watching everyone else look calm, which can make a real emergency seem like a false alarm to everyone at once. The bystander must then decide that they personally bear some responsibility to act, judge that they know how to help, and finally decide to actually act. A breakdown at any one of these steps, not just the responsibility step, can stop someone from helping, and the presence of other people can interfere at more than one of these steps at once.
